full_name: Princeton AI Alignment + Safety (AIAS) & POLARIS Lab
mission: Princeton AI Alignment + Safety 'is a research initiative focused on the scientific foundations of AI alignment', drawing on ML, theoretical CS, game theory, optimisation, control and economics. It launched with a symposium on 19 Oct 2026, directed by Elad Hazan with Mark Braverman as associate director. It builds on existing Princeton safety work such as Peter Henderson's POLARIS Lab (law + AI safety) and the PASS seminar.

key_work.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep
key_work.plain_summary: Explains why chatbots are easy to jailbreak — their safety mostly lives in the first few words of a reply — and proposes 'deeper' alignment; ICLR 2025 Outstanding Paper.

key_work.title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
key_work.plain_summary: Showed a few fine-tuning examples can strip safety training from aligned models, even accidentally.

key_work.title: Dynamic Risk Assessments for Offensive Cybersecurity Agents
key_work.plain_summary: POLARIS Lab shows adversaries with modest compute can significantly boost AI hacking agents, so static evaluations underestimate risk.

key_work.title: Statutory Construction and Interpretation for Artificial Intelligence
key_work.plain_summary: Argues ambiguity in the 'laws' (constitutions, specs) we give AI is a core alignment problem and borrows tools from legal interpretation.

warnings.text: 'AI is getting more and more capable very rapidly, and we have few mechanisms in place to make it a safe technology' (Elad Hazan at launch).
Model safety isn't fixed: adversaries can adapt open or fine-tunable models, creating a 'bubble' of risk that static audits miss (POLARIS Lab).
Current safety alignment is shallow and easily bypassed by jailbreaks or fine-tuning.

recommendations.text: Make safety evaluations dynamic, compute-aware and continually updated (POLARIS).
Build deeper safety alignment that lets models recover from an initial failure.
Develop rigorous foundations for evaluating and overseeing systems that may exceed human capabilities (AIAS agenda).
